value: TRIPLE STRAP: centre straight, two lateral curved like the horns of a crescent
note: The author's own type-definition. 'One of the most resisting, and therefore prevalent forms, appears to have been a triple strap, the centre straight, and the lateral curved like the horns of a crescent.'

value: security
note: All three straps spring from BEHIND the stonework when the door is closed, 'made it particularly difficult to wrench off'. Function drives the form; the triple count was ALSO read as symbolic.

value: extra crescents sprung from or butted onto the central strap
note: 'Sometimes one or two additional crescents spring from the central strap, or are butted on to it.'

value: the terminals
note: 'The ends of these straps are often beaten into scrolls and foliage, WHOSE FASHION IS AN INDICATION OF AGE, WHICH THE FORM ALONE FAILS TO CONVEY.' So date the hinge by its terminal, not its silhouette.

value: rudimentary leaves / dragons' heads in high relief / profile heads with distended jaws / 'a usual Frankish tongue between two scrolls'
note: Named terminal vocabulary. The Frankish-tongue-between-two-scrolls is the Montreal type.

value: crescent hinge with split and scrolled ends, very early 11th c.
note: Evidenced by a Saxon carving from Selsey, now in Chichester Cathedral - a CARVING used to date ironwork.
The two St Albans-related doors, giving hard anchors for the scrolled-terminal style.

value: small detached crescents and straps, much piercing, arranged in patterns
note: Finest at Pontigny (fig 25); spread to Montreal, Chablis, Cologne (St Ursula); densest in Aquitaine and Auvergne. On cathedral doors of Angers the pieces are placed in RANDOM patterns.

value: three bands per door, each a crescent plus a circle of BROAD IRON WITH UPTURNED EDGES enclosing filigree
note: Montreal, Yonne (fig 26). Explicitly compared to 'contemporary goldsmiths' work'. Reappears near Brunswick a century later.

value: lobes of the leaves SUNK; larger veins and the periphery RAISED; stems usually GROOVED
note: A precise surface spec for foliate ironwork, from the Rouen/Noyon vine style. Typical 13th-c. vine, sometimes replaced by a trefoil or cinquefoil vine, always mingled with rosette-like flowers and sometimes fruit (grapes).

value: stamped work, lavishly used
note: At St Denis. Matches the Eleanor grille's repeated-unit construction - richness by repetition of forged/stamped elements, not by unique freehand work.

value: lay (non-monastic) architecture -> simpler, more restrained hinges
note: Per Viollet-le-Duc, beginning in the Royal Domain. A usable style parameter that is not about date.

value: provincial style lags; do not date by style outside metropolitan centres
note: 'fashions penetrated so slowly in the past, that it is impossible, without great local knowledge, to predicate the date of any work from its style, where the style is not indigenous.' Cites Icelandic carving still resembling the Bayeux Tapestry within living memory.

value: fourteen important surviving specimens, plausibly one craftsman's tour
note: Eaton Bray and Turvey (Beds), Norwich, Tunstall, Windsor, Oxford, Lichfield, York, Chester, Westminster - grouped by plausible travel, with Westminster needing 'a special journey'.

value: heat confined to preliminary stages; the greater part of the work done by file and saw or by embossing
note: Verbatim: "Heat was now applied only in the preliminary stages, and the greater part of the work was accomplished by the file and saw, or by embossing the iron". Hedged — "the greater part", not all. The book never uses the word "cold"; that is an inference. p.115 prints no folio (chapter-opening page); the page number is fixed by the Contents entry and the "116" running head on the next leaf.

value: carving the object from the solid is reserved for the top tier only
note: when the highest realms of art were reached, by carving the statuette or other decorative object from the solid — a tier marker, not a routine finishing step.

value: direct forge and hammer products largely excluded from the design
note: The direct productions of the forge and hammer were seldom admitted into the design. Licenses a different surface vocabulary for 15th-16th c. props: crisp filed arrises, saw-cut piercing, sunk and chased detail, no hammer scale or fire-welded lumps.

value: the locksmith needs construction, planning, and the arts of the armourer and jeweller
note: Same page: to be accomplished it "was requisite to understand construction and planning, and to be an adept in the arts of the locksmith, the armourer, and the jeweller". OCR-derived line, not image-verified.

value: sheet iron becomes the general material
note: The use of sheet iron became general — the sentence straddles the p.115/116 break and p.116 back-refers to "This use of sheet iron".

value: hinges built of several thicknesses of sheet iron, pierced to represent tracery, riveted together in strong frames
note: Verbatim and image-verified. Emit lattice member and cell filler as separate meshes with separate materials.

value: layer count 1 to 3-4 superimposed pierced sheets, as a joint richness and date axis
note: Exemplar of a single thickness given: the guichet in the south choir aisle at Chartres, "pierced in only one thickness"; "increasing richness of design soon demanded the use of three or four sheets of piercing superimposed". Scoped to France, 15th c.

value: top tier is NOT laminated sheet: crockets, pinnacles and leading lines chiselled and filed from solid iron in full relief
note: Verbatim, image-verified: pierced sheet-work "plays but a very subordinate part". CORRECTION APPLIED — the earlier claim called the pierced sheet a "backing"; the book does not say that, and the word has been dropped. Scope is comparative ("all these grander works") and tied to the Rouen and Evreux examples, not to medieval ironwork generally.

value: small work outranks large: locks and knockers reach a refinement "hardly surpassed by the contemporary work in gold and silver"
note: Quality hierarchy runs opposite to size. Useful for deciding where to spend polygon and texture budget.

value: assembly model is joinery in iron
note: the caps, bases, mouldings, crockets, and cusps are chased out of the solid, and tenoned, morticed, and riveted together as in joinery. Depth and richness are given by using one thickness upon another, over a background of saw-pierced sheet iron. The best assembly spec in the chapter and the direct explanation of fig 45.

value: rim-lock anatomy: front plate, back plate, bolts, latches
note: Front plate "more or less decorated with scroll-work"; back plate, by which the lock is fastened to the door, "extended beyond the lock, and cut into leaves, animals' heads, fleurs-de-lis, and other forms". The extended-and-cut back plate is the shaped silhouette seen in figs 49 and 51. Rim-locks richly ornamented "as early as the thirteenth century".

value: master-keys with tracery handles and innumerable wards
note: The only warding reference in the chapter, and it is a count, not a geometry.

value: mechanism deliberately conceals bolts and keyholes
note: their mechanism is careful, concealing bolts and key-holes with great skill — explains why not one figure in chapter V shows a bolt, ward, hasp or shackle.

value: pierced-and-applied tracery panels pinned by small rivet clips over a plain backplate
note: Fig 45: three discrete panels, each pinned by four clips of 3-4 rivet dots at the quarter points, with the border cable visible between panels.

value: splayed lock type — plate flaring to its base on concave ogee sides
note: The book's own type name, applied explicitly in the p.137 paragraph illustrated by figs 49-51 ("The splayed locks peculiar to Germany were often treated thus"). Extending it to fig 48 is an inference from silhouette, not a quotation.

value: keyhole forms: plain round eye with tapering triangular slot; cruciform/anchor slot for a cross-warded key
note: Fig 45 plain, fig 51 cruciform with a round hole at the foot. The keyhole silhouette is itself a typology signal.

value: buttress-shaped hasp, rude and uniform, on the Brabançon export boxes
note: uniformly rude and ill-designed buttress-shaped hasp and decoration; this identity rendering it probable that they were produced in one centre and abundantly exported. The only hasp description in the chapter.

value: French sheet-iron coffer recipe: strapped, trunk-curved lid, stacked pierced panels, buttress projections of two or three stages, angle buttresses lengthened into legs
note: formed of thin pierced metal plates laid over each other with great neatness, with projecting pieces shaped like buttresses of two or three stages, those at the angles being lengthened into legs on which the casket stands; "all were painted and gilt". Close of the 14th c.

value: two-part system: straps forming the lattice, pierced-and-embossed plates filling the interspaces
note: The book's own vocabulary — "lining entire doors with pierced and embossed plates and straps of iron" — maps directly onto the generator split.

value: period term for the lattice member: "banded iron"; nails "shaped into rosettes"
note: Confirmed by eye in fig 54, where each flat bar is edged on both margins by a cable/rope-twist bead.

value: painted-ground variant: charges painted on the woodwork between iron straps
note: sometimes merely painted on the woodwork between the iron straps. Cheap iron, rich paint.

value: embossed-iron variant: armorials "splendidly embossed in iron"
note: Krems. Same lattice generator, different cell filler.

value: non-repeating plate designs require a grammar, not a library
note: few of the designs being repeated. Bruck's economics are the inverse of the other three doors.

value: lattice angle is a genuine variable, not always 45 degrees
note: Scan-derived: about 45deg at Cracow, 46deg (treat as 45) at Karlstein, 50.9deg at Bruck, 54.3deg at Krems. Band width as a fraction of crossing pitch varies far more: 0.16 Karlstein, 0.17 Bruck, 0.25 Cracow (of perpendicular spacing), 0.38 Krems.

value: nail placement is diagnostic: crossings bare at Cracow, rosette at every crossing at Bruck and Karlstein
note: Cracow: ring nail at every plate centre, quatrefoil at every segment midpoint, crossings bare. Bruck: identical rosette at both crossings and midpoints. Karlstein: whirl at every crossing, cross-in-roundel rows along the straps.

value: border band sweeps continuously round rounded shoulders; the repeat bends along the arc, no corner block, no mitre
note: Contrast fig 45's lock border, where the cable direction reverses at each corner.

value: clipping rule: iron is cut hard at the edge, painted charges are re-fitted to partial cells
note: Cracow's diaper is simply clipped by the arch curve; Karlstein's bottom half-lozenges contain compressed but complete eagles and lions.

value: Karlstein border nail sequence is period-3: whirl, cross, cross, with a whirl at each corner
note: Verified along a 900 px strip. Two nail types only, plus the field studs.

value: Krems double checkerboard plus a mid-height subject swap
note: Boss-at-crossing versus figure-in-interspace; griffin versus arms within the interspaces above; imperial eagles and lions below. Four figure plates and one boss cover the whole door.

value: tabernacle-door variant uses RECTANGULAR interstices, filled with carved tracery, filigree, or pierced and embossed subjects
note: The main bars were always massive, though often almost wholly concealed by pierced foliage and arabesques. Fig 57 (located only) is the example; its subjects are "taken, in part at least, from the New Testament".

value: the diaper family is said to derive from Belgian and German trellised tabernacle-door grilles, enriched eastward with rosettes at the bar intersections
note: Gardner's own transmission account for this family, offered without documentary support — treat as his hypothesis.

value: the effects of wood and stone are produced in iron in miniature
note: OCR-derived, not image-verified. Attributed to the combined smith, clockmaker and architect bringing "the more precise, cultivated, and elaborated tools of the mechanician" to bear.

value: the design basis of all these locks is "the flamboyant architecture of the period"
note: Image-verified. So the lock generator should be driven by a tracery generator, not by an ornament library.

value: full miniature-building vocabulary occurs on a single lock plate
note: Fig 48: dentil/battlement cap, arcaded gallery of about seven bays, crocketed gablets, pendant leaf frieze, moulded string courses, four pinnacled buttress strips, crocketed ogee gables, ranks of about six cusped lancets, a transom band of quatrefoils-in-square. At 18 inches overall the lancets scale to roughly 6-8 mm.

value: miniature guichets: "most exquisite little circular guichets filled with flamboyant tracery of a great variety of design"
note: OCR-derived. St Pierre, Louvain. A small round tracery-panel asset with high variation, fitted to armoire doors.

value: Gardner treats the transposition of wood and stone forms into iron as the CAUSE of decline
note: OCR-derived: the East sent "the wave of fashion which required the smith to produce in iron the wood lattice and the pierced marble window, forms proper to wood and stone, by which his art declined". This is an aesthetic verdict, not evidence; see oriental_influence.

value: pierced and slightly embossed sheet-iron, brightly TINNED, laid over RED cloth or paper
note: The single most useful material line in the chapters: "in which the iron was brightly tinned and laid over red cloth or paper. The splayed locks peculiar to Germany were often treated thus, as in the Rathhaus of Cologne, of Bingen, and elsewhere on the Rhine." Two materials, not one monochrome metal. "Sea-weed-looking" is the author's own term for the arabesque of fig 51.

value: gilding is the default, not an option
note: Windsor group: "The whole was originally gilt" (p.128, image-verified). French coffers: "all were painted and gilt" (p.119). Bare dark iron is the wrong default for this material class.

value: gilt iron over lozenge grounds painted alternately red and blue
note: The ground of the lozenges was painted alternately red and blue, so that the general effect was like gold lace on a scarlet-and-blue chequer. Bruck. A two-tone cell colour is a cheap, high-impact texture parameter.

value: Karlstein tinctures fully specified
note: the black eagle of Austria on gold alternates with the silver lion of Bohemia on red. The iron straps are fixed by well-modelled nails, and decorated with gold-and-black rosettes. Directly usable material values.

value: door-linings "illuminated in black and white, red and blue, and profusely gilded"
note: OCR-derived. Palette spec for the whole door-lining family.

value: embossing height is a variable independent of pattern density, and high relief tends to regularise the layout
note: OCR-derived: Nuremberg hinges "embossed to an unusual height, and assuming, as frequently happens, an almost geometric arrangement". A useful coupling rule.

value: NEGATIVE FINDING: no etching and no cast iron anywhere in chapter V
note: The finishing processes named are gilding, tinning (p.137 only) and painting or illuminating in colour. "Cast" appears only for plaster casts held by the South Kensington Museum. Do not give 15th-16th c. ironwork assets an etched or cast finish on this book's authority.

value: file, saw, chisel
note: The core locksmith triad. p.126 (OCR) adds "produced works by aid of the file, saw, and chisel on the grandest scale".

value: vandyked (deeply zigzag-indented) edges, produced by punching and filing
note: p.116, image-verified: the St Bertin (St Omer) door plates are "horizontal and overlapping" with "edges vandyked in exactly the same pattern as the plate armour then worn"; Auxerre's hinges are "long straps with thin vandyked edges". p.110 gives the process: bands "punched and filed into key-borders, crenelations, or vandyked edgings" — subtractive. CORRECTION APPLIED: Gardner asserts identical pattern and contemporaneity with plate armour, NOT that the smith copied armour; "copied from" was an inference and has been withdrawn. He also never defines "vandyked" — the zigzag gloss is modern.

value: interlaced hoop-iron door bands fixed by "rosettes or decorated nails", with lozenge interstices filled by sheet ornament
note: Image-verified. This is the ancestor of the fig 53-56 lattice systems. Note the nail statement is made of the band type generally, not specifically of the vandyked St Bertin plates.

value: incised lines, twisted and notched mouldings
note: Three cheap, tileable edge treatments for bars and mouldings. Instances: the nicked chamfer on fig 50's top edge, the cable border of fig 45, the cable-edged bands of fig 54.

value: embossing, and chasing "as if in silver"
note: p.118, image-verified: the figures of saints and kings, masks, and escutcheons of arms are "chiselled out of solid iron and chased as if in silver".

value: stamping belongs to the earlier French school, not to the locksmith tier
note: OCR-derived. Stamped leafy terminations, stamped heads and rosettes, stamped rosettes used as nail-heads; p.114 says German architectural ironwork designs were "entirely based on the rich stamped work of France". Keep stamping for 13th-14th c. assets and file/saw/chisel for 15th-16th c.

value: pouncing, piercing and lining of broad surfaces and edges
note: OCR-derived, on door-handles: "their broad surfaces and edges being pounced, pierced, lined". Adds pouncing (dot punching) to the vocabulary — visible in the dot rows of figs 45, 49 and 50.

value: vizzying / guichet — small viewing wicket in a door
note: p.129, image-verified: "On the south door of the ambulatory is a 'vizzying,' or guichet, a square escutcheon, and a handle-plate in form of a rose window surrounded by the Garter".

value: escutcheon; handle-plate; back-plate
note: The door-furniture set that ships alongside a lock. German specialities include "tracery back-plates" (p.132).

value: wattle border / iron wattlework (Flemish)
note: OCR-derived; the figure (fig 46) is located only, not examined.

value: banded iron; nails shaped into rosettes
note: The lattice member and nail type of the sheathed-door family.

value: diploma work — a guild qualification masterpiece
note: Image-verified. The legitimate name for a hero prop.

value: corona; herse-light; pricket
note: OCR-derived. Corona = a hanging light ring; prickets are the candle spikes.

value: brattishing, crocket, cusp, transom, lancet, ogee
evidence: stated p.128 (crockets, cusps) and inferred elsewhere
note: Only "crockets, pinnacles, mouldings, caps, bases, cusps" are the book's words (p.128). The rest of the architectural terms used in the figure notes are standard modern descriptive vocabulary, not Gardner's — do not cite him for them.

value: locks: best in DESIGN at the close of the fifteenth century, increasing in RICHNESS through the sixteenth
note: Verbatim and image-verified: "The best in design belong to the close of the fifteenth century, but they increase in richness during the sixteenth." Stated flatly, no hedge. Scoped by context to French and Flemish flamboyant lock-plate work. Tie a richness slider to date: restrained and well-composed = c.1480-1500, over-loaded = 16th c.

value: Germany: the thistle enters from the beginning of the sixteenth century and ousts the vine
note: OCR-derived: "for a century no ironwork of any pretension was forged in Germany into the composition of which the thistle did not enter." Vine up to c.1500, thistle c.1500-1600. Figs 49, 50 and 51 are thistle-derived and so read 16th c. by this rule, while fig 48 (pure tracery, no thistle) reads 15th.

value: late-thistle markers: leaves take a definite cruciform shape and keep it to the end; in extreme degeneration only cross-hatching survives "the last trace of the calyx"
note: Two generator flags: leaf_shape = cruciform (late) and calyx = crosshatch_only (very late). The stippled cross-hatched calyx is visible on both thistle heads of fig 49.

value: trellis threading topology: oldest German work threads all bars of one direction through the other; the later, more ponderous Magdeburg door of 1495 threads them alternately
note: OCR-derived but the sentence is clean: Cologne and Aix-la-Chapelle for the older form.

value: bar section: fifteenth-century trellis is made "with square instead of round iron"
note: The sentence runs across the fig 57 page: p.143 ends "in being made with square instead" and p.145 opens "of round iron. It seems as if the German smiths were already courting difficulties in order to display their skill." Square = 15th c., round = the familiar work of a century later.

value: Austrian door-linings: none older than the fifteenth century, and the custom outlasted the arrival of Renaissance architecture
note: OCR-derived. Cracow examples "the latter half of the fifteenth century"; Krems and its relatives at Carinthia and Steier "towards the close of the fifteenth century" (p.142).

value: the Passion-flower type belongs to the Renaissance, not the Gothic
note: OCR-derived. Fully developed form is "a spindle-shaped coil of wire for the pistil, with elongated hammer-shaped stamens, and slender recurved petals", elaborated out of the twelfth-century fleur-de-lis. Do not put it on a 15th-c. asset.

value: Flemish and Brabançon locks, handles and door-knockers are "sturdier and plainer than the French"
note: Image-verified. Bar thickness up, detail count down.

value: German traceried work: delicate tracery, coarse architecture
note: while the tracery is delicate, the buttresses and pinnacles are intolerably coarse. Detail count up, moulding refinement down. Three presets over one generator: French (both refinements up), Flemish (plainer and heavier), German (denser and coarser).

value: German specialities: open tracery handles "of Saracenic outline", tracery back-plates, and intertwining leafless branching handles
note: OCR-derived. "Leafless branching" is a distinct stem grammar from the leafy thistle scroll. Treat "Saracenic outline" as Gardner's shorthand for a look, not a provenance claim.

value: the trellis diaper is "as distinctive of German smithing as the thistle"
note: OCR-derived, and adds a transmission claim: "evidently first borrowed by Belgium from the sparse examples of England and France".

value: door-linings of pierced and embossed plates and straps are an Austrian, Bohemian and Polish speciality
note: OCR-derived. The four sheathed doors are all from this zone (Cracow, Bruck on the Mur, Karlstein, Krems).

value: the pierced-sheet lamination recipe is scoped to France and the fifteenth century
note: Same passage says the English smith "had ceased to lead the way, and fashioned little but the rudest work", while the French smith "assimilated the methods and skill of the locksmith and armourer to his own". Do not apply it pan-European.

value: guild qualification piece: the 18-inch Maria-Saal lock-plate "is regarded as having been a diploma work"
note: Image-verified. Gives the social category for a showpiece asset, and the only hard lock dimension in the chapters.

value: a trade corporation commissioned and donated major church ironwork
note: OCR-derived: the corona made by Gert Bulsinck of Vreden in 1489 was "presented to the church by the Corporation of Locksmiths" — two pierced sheet-iron bands carrying canopied niches with figures of saints and a candle in front of each, a gilded wood Virgin under a wrought canopy at the centre, two kneeling figures above.

value: combined trades in one person: smith, clockmaker and architect
note: OCR-derived. Josse Matsys of Louvain was municipal architect, clockmaker and blacksmith; his son Quentin (b.1466) is the painter. p.126 links the combination directly to the precision of the work.

value: uniform design across exported goods used to infer a single production centre
note: Image-verified reasoning about the Brabançon boxes: "this identity rendering it probable that they were produced in one centre and abundantly exported". A period-appropriate way to justify asset reuse across a map region.

value: named hands to chase
note: A. F. Butsch (the richest pierced-thistle locks, Soyter Collection and the chapel at Blutenbourg near Munich, p.137, image-verified); Gert Bulsinck of Vreden (1489 corona, p.134); Josse Matsys of Louvain, Antwerp well-cover dated 1470 (p.122); Jean de Cuyper, Mechlin market rails, 1531 (p.121).

value: 1893 collectors' market value, not a period price
note: over £1000 has been paid for a single specimen. Evidence of Victorian valuation only — do not use as a medieval price.

value: Gardner's thesis, as a chapter title: "The Transition, due to Oriental Influence in the Fourteenth Century"
note: The causation is built into the book's structure, so it cannot be quietly ignored when citing chapter IV.

value: claimed transfer of TOOLS and PROCESSES from the East
note: OCR-derived: "From the East the smith learnt to use the file and saw, and the sumptuous arts of graving, inlaying with gold and silver, damascening and embossing" (OCR prints "gravmg"). Asserted; no object, workshop, treatise or craftsman is cited in support.

value: claimed transfer of FORMS: iron grilles as strength-copies of pierced Saracenic marble
note: OCR-derived: "The first attempts consist of a few grilles, copies (for the sake of strength) in iron of the pierced marble so extensively used in Saracenic archit[e]cture; and, emanating from our instructors in geometry, they are naturally geometric in design." Named examples: St Anastasia's, Verona and St Mark's, Venice, "probably as old as the thirteenth" century. The phrase "our instructors in geometry" shows the argument is being carried by rhetoric.

value: the evidence offered is overwhelmingly eye-judged resemblance
note: a rich and essentially Saracenic diaper (p.105); "It is unquestionably an Eastern design" (p.105, of the Canterbury grille contracted to Roger Johnson of London in 1428); handles "which might have been taken straight from the mosque" (p.109). No dated intermediate objects, no documented imports, no craftsman movements.

value: one genuinely evidential datum, and it proves contact rather than design transmission
note: OCR-derived: a plate at Rendcombe, Gloucestershire "has Arabic numerals and figures engraved upon it, presenting their supposed earliest use in any work connected with building". Note "supposed". Numerals travel with notation and commerce; they do not demonstrate that the ornament was copied from Islamic sources.

value: one supporting item is explicit hearsay
note: The Pamplona cloister grille (dated 1212) "is said to have been made from Moorish chains". Gardner reports it as report.

value: Gardner undercuts his own thesis when he actually reasons about a mechanism
note: OCR-derived, on pierced sunk-work: the leaves are "beaten out thin and flat, and the sunk parts pierced right through, giving the work an entirely novel and rather Oriental effect. It is just the sort of rendering we might get from a smith, set to work from a drawing without sections, and unacquainted with the process of stamping." Here a purely local, mundane cause is offered for the very look he elsewhere attributes to the East. The strongest internal reason to treat the diffusion claim as unproven.

value: the thesis does double duty as a value judgement
note: Credit for tools, blame for decline: the same page says the Eastern fashion required iron to imitate wood and stone forms, "by which his art declined". A 19th-century diffusionist and hierarchical frame, not a finding.

value: usable residue for the factory
note: Keep the FORMS as design-family labels and drop the causation: geometric interlace grille (Verona, Venice); the halved-and-riveted diagonal notched-strap diaper (Canterbury choir side entrance, with the same design in wood at Luxeuil); the flattened-ellipse handle ring "shaped like a crescent with the horns beaten round to join the spindle" (p.109). Do not label assets "Saracenic" or "Oriental" on this book's authority, and do not put the causal claim into asset metadata.
